title: The seventy-two (Luke 10:1–24)
hook: sent in pairs like lambs among wolves, peace to this house

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus set his face toward Jerusalem, and the foxes had holes. Your line was no looking back. Did you take the first step? Day four hundred sixty.

In many Catholic homes, sometime around the Epiphany in January, someone climbs on a chair with a piece of blessed chalk and writes over the front door: the year, split in two, with three letters in the middle, C, M and B, joined by crosses. People read the letters as the names tradition gives the three wise men, and also as the start of a Latin blessing: may Christ bless this house. Guests walk under it all year. It's a small, homemade custom. Its roots run back to a road in Luke, where Jesus sends out a crowd of ordinary disciples and tells them the first thing to say at every door. Today, the seventy-two.
screen: `CHALK OVER THE FRONT DOOR.` → `MAY CHRIST BLESS THIS HOUSE.` → `THE FIRST THING TO SAY AT A DOOR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday he set his face toward Jerusalem. Now he sends people ahead of him. Not just the twelve this time. The Douay-Rheims says the Lord appointed "other seventy-two: and he sent them two and two before his face into every city and place whither he himself was to come." Two and two, so nobody goes alone. Then the honest warning: "behold I send you as lambs among wolves." No purse, no bag, no sandals, no stopping to chat on the road. And at every door, one sentence first: "Into whatsoever house you enter, first say: Peace be to this house." If someone there is a child of peace, Jesus says, your peace will rest on him. If not, it will come back to you. You can't waste a blessing. It either lands or returns. Peace in Jesus' language is shalom: not just quiet, but wholeness, everything as it should be. The number is a puzzle. Some ancient manuscripts say seventy, some say seventy-two, which is why your Bible may differ from the Douay. Scholars note that the list of the world's nations in Genesis chapter ten has seventy names in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. Either way, the number seems to say: this message is for everyone. And the ending is pure joy. The seventy-two come back thrilled: even the devils obey us! Jesus says rejoice in something better, that your names are written in heaven. Catholics take this as the first sending of the ordinary faithful, not just the apostles. Anyone can walk to a door two by two and say peace.
screen: `TWO AND TWO, BEFORE HIS FACE.` · `LAMBS AMONG WOLVES.` · `A BLESSING LANDS OR RETURNS.` · `SEVENTY OR SEVENTY-TWO.` · then, large: `PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless a house you enter. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next door you'll walk through today: your own front door, an office, a classroom, a friend's apartment, a hospital room. Picture yourself at its threshold. Before you step in, imagine wishing peace on everyone inside, the ones you love and the ones you don't. You don't need to say it aloud. If you pray, you can say Jesus' own words silently: peace be to this house. Then picture walking in lighter. The bell holds the time.
The seventy-two. The wider circle of disciples Jesus sent out two by two, as lambs among wolves, with peace as their first word at every door. Today's word.
Your line: peace be to this house. Today, say it silently at every threshold you cross, and watch where it lands. Day four hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Many Catholic families bless their homes at Epiphany by chalking the year and the letters C+M+B over the door, and priests often begin a house blessing with Jesus' words, peace be to this house.

fork.setup: you're one of the seventy-two. you knock on a stranger's door in a town you've never seen. what do you say first?
options: ask if they'll let you stay.
fork.reveal: Jesus tells them to say it first, before anything. if it isn't received, the peace comes back to them.

original.note: Greek: peace. Behind it stands the Hebrew shalom, wholeness, everything as it should be.

trapdoor: what you thought: the seventy-two were a fixed group of junior apostles.
what it means: they're a wider circle of disciples Jesus sends ahead in pairs, carrying peace to every house.
what a scholar hears: manuscripts split between seventy and seventy-two; Genesis 10 lists seventy nations in Hebrew and seventy-two in the Greek Septuagint.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 10:1, 10:3 and 10:5 (including 'seventy-two' with hyphen).
Manuscript variation seventy/seventy-two and the Genesis 10 table of nations (70 in the Masoretic text, 72 in the Septuagint) is a standard note; confirm counts.
Epiphany chalk custom: C+M+B read as Caspar, Melchior, Balthasar and as Christus mansionem benedicat; confirm.
'The first sending of the ordinary faithful' is interpretive; confirm phrasing fits Catholic reading.
